speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Lithuania became an independent democratic nation on February 16, 1918. It lost that status in 1940 when the country was occupied by the U.S.S.R. Today Lithuanians who live in the free world celebrate their independence day. Therefore, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Edmonton South (Mr. Roche):
That this House recognize the sixty-second anniversary of the declaration of the independence of Lithuania, and join with those Lithuanians who seek an end to Soviet aggression and a return of Lithuania to a free and democratic society.

That this House congratulate the organizers of the Conference on Women and the Constitution who mobilized, in less than two weeks, this forceful and effective demonstration of women's determination to achieve full equality in our Canadian society.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to introduce the following motion. In spite of the fact that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) has been notified for some time that there has been no anaesthetist and no back-up surgeon at the federally run Inuvik General Hospital since Christmas, thereby not only forcing general surgery patients but also maternity cases to be evacuated to Edmonton some 1,300 miles away, and because the situation remains unchanged and critical, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp):

subsubtopic: CONDITIONS IN ARCTIC QUEBEC-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Over five years have lapsed since the signing of the James Bay and northern Quebec agreement. Subsection 29.0.30 of that agreement states that Canada and Quebec shall, together with the Inuit communities, undertake studies respecting air services, as soon as possible. The conditions of airstrips in northern Quebec are below standard. The Akulivik airstrip is 366 metres by 30 metres, Beilin 350 metres by 20 metres, and in Port-Nouveau-Quebec the airstrip has been classified by the Quebec government as dangerous. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton):
That the Minister of Transport initiate studies on air services in Arctic Quebec immediately, and that he take responsibility for rectifying the deplorable conditions that exist there.

speechtext:

Borrowing Authority

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY

speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, February 12, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bussieres (for the Minister of Finance) that Bill C-59, to provide supplementary borrowing authority, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

speakeroldname: Mr. John Evans (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today 1 want to try to respond to some of the allegations made earlier in the debate by members of the official opposition and of the New Democratic Party with respect to Bill C-59. For example, that the government is asking for a blank cheque in this bill; that the government is requesting more borrowing authority than it needs; that the government has not put forward a plan for restraint of expenditures, as the minister indicated earlier, and that deficits will not be reduced under the plan forward which has, in turn, led to the borrowing authority bill.
In addition, during a number of days of debate allegations have been put forward by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) and other members of the opposition comparing the December, 1979, budget introduced by the hon. member for St. John's West in the previous government and the budget put forward by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) on October 28.
I want to show through analysis that the kinds of assertions made-namely, that the 1979 budget would have led to a lower deficit, a greater reduction in financial requirement and generally a more responsible fiscal pattern-are fallacious. As well, I want to look at the commitment which the government has put forward regarding a change of priorities in the budget toward greater emphasis on economic and energy development. Finally, I want to respond to some specific criticisms put forward by the opposition of the government's program during the debate on Bill C-59.
First let me deal with the question put forward by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), a question repeated subsequently. Opposition members say the government is asking for a blank cheque, that it is asking for $14 billion with no plan and with no knowledge by members opposite as to what use the $14 billion will be put. That assertion by members opposite is total nonsense. In his budget of October 28 the Minister of Finance put forward the most comprehensive description of a government's expenditure plans of any government in the history of this House. The budget clearly showed the expenditure plans by category or envelope for this year and the next two years. It is clear from the budget document presented by the minister on October 28 that this $14 billion is needed for the government's expenditure plan. It is clearly laid out in that document. The idea that it is a blank cheque and that the opposition is given no indication where the expenditures will occur is pure rhetoric.
In addition, we will soon be considering the estimates for 1981-82. At that time we will have very detailed descriptions of what each department within the over-all envelope structure will be using the moneys sought in the borrowing authority for under the expenditure plan.
I commend the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) for what has been brought forward just recently. I refer to the beginnings of what will be a complete revision of the public accounts of Canada and a much more detailed description than we have had in the past with regard to government expenditure programs, even more detailed than what is now available.
Therefore, the argument that the government is asking for a blank cheque, that it simply does not want the public to know how it is going to spend the moneys asked for in the bill before us today, is pure rhetoric. It has no basis in fact. That argument simply cannot stand the test of fact.
An assertion was put forward by the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) with respect to his belief that in this bill we were asking for some $5.9 billion more than was needed by the government under the proposed expenditure plan. That simply is not true. As of March 31, 1981, as I explained to the hon. member opposite, all existing borrowing authority will have expired. In other words, no borrowing authority will be carried forward into fiscal year 1981-82 from previous fiscal years.
There was unused borrowing authority in the budget presented by the hon. member for St. John's West which was carried over from the budget in 1978. At the time borrowing authority was requested, $2.9 billion of non-lapsing borrowing authority was carried forward into 1979. When the hon. member for St. John's West presented his budget in 1979, he had this unused borrowing authority.
It was carried forward after the election into the 1980-81 election year because the government's borrowing authority bill was not passed until July, 1980. The government ran between March 31, 1980, and that point in July on that unlapsed $2.9 billion borrowing authority. At that time it was completely exhausted. When the borrowing authority bill of last summer passed, there was $100 million of unlapsed borrowing authority. Therefore, to all intents and purposes there was no borrowing authority left.
The borrowing authority that was requested and granted by the House last summer will lapse in its entirety, if not used, as of March 31, 1981. Therefore, there is no existing borrowing authority that will be carried on to the next year. That being the case, and given the fact that from the budget our fiscal year 1981-82 financial requirements are $11 billion, the borrowing authority of $14 billion, subtracting the $11 billion-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, rather than try to recall off the top of my head the answer to that question, we will commit that when the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres) speaks tonight to close the debate, he will have that information for the hon. member.
As I was saying with regard to the $11 billion of financial requirements for 1981-82-page 41 of the budget speech, if the hon. member is interested in looking at it-we are now asking for $14 billion of which $3 billion will be non-lapsing. In other words, the government is asking for $3 billion of the $14 billion to be non-lapsing to the extent that on March 31, 1982, that sum would not expire. It will be carried over into fiscal year 1982-83 after March 31.
The reason is to allow flexibility from the rigid 12-month borrowing authority rules. If the government could not get borrowing authority for 1982-83 passed by March 31, 1982, the government would have borrowing authority to operate on until such time as that bill could be passed. That is an extremely valuable flexibility.
In fiscal year 1980-81, at which time we had an election, we found that with the $2.9 billion of unused borrowing authority that was non-lapsing from the budget of the previous minister of finance in 1979 the government could keep going until it could introduce legislation to get borrowing authority for the new fiscal year. That is why we are asking for the non-lapsing portion.
That $3 billion of extra borrowing authority over and above our projected financial requirements is required for two purposes. First, it is to provide some degree of flexibility to ensure that we have enough borrowing authority to cover contingencies that may arise should the projections not be exactly as we have forecast. Second, that borrowing authority would be available to be used for foreign currency transactions which could be required in the event of a need to support the value of the currency, for example. For all these reasons, it is typical for governments to request somewhat more borrowing authority than they have the intention of borrowing for their financial projections in the budget.
That has been the case in the past. It is the case with this borrowing authority. I think the hon. member for Mississauga South now understands that the excessive $5.9 billion request that he was discussing earlier was under the assumption that we still had the $2.9 billion of unused borrowing authority from the 1978 budget that was non-lapsing. I think he understands that is not the case.
I think I have been able to show in this short period that we are not asking for a blank cheque or for an unnecessarily large amount, given the financial requirements that are projected. That is not to say we would not like to see the financial requirements be much less; but using realistic estimates, we are in the position where that is going to be the likely amount of financing that will have to be done by the government to finance governmental operations in fiscal year 1981-82. It is
Borrowing Authority
clear from the budgetary documents precisely what those funds will be used for.
There has been an accusation that the deficits of this government will continue to grow, that in effect there is no commitment on the part of the government to reduce the deficit or to restrain expenditures. That accusation has been made by a great many members on the other side of the House. I wish to state in the strongest possible terms that this is in fact false. The government has every intention, every commitment, to bring the deficit down in the future, starting this year-

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: You have been saying that for ten years.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
-and to keep the growth of expenditures over the next three years within the average growth rate of the gross national product. That commitment has been made by the Minister of Finance and the Minister of State for Finance on a number of occasions. I can assure the House that this commitment is solid, that it is firm; it is a commitment which the government and the Minister of Finance are completely and totally committed to keeping to the people of Canada.
If we look at the situation, I think all governments have to operate on the basis of financial projection. The hon. member for St. John's West, when he was minister of finance, put forward his projections. All governments put forward their best estimate of how they are going to be able to finance in the forthcoming period. That does not mean that that is an absolute certainty and that that is the way the world is going to unfold; it means that at this point in time it is the best possible estimate of how we will do in the next financial period. In the set of projections that we have put forward in the budget, we find that the financial requirements will decline from a level of $12.2 billion in 1980-81, which is the present fiscal year, to a level of $7.2 billion in fiscal year 1983-84. That is a $5 billion reduction, and I note, in passing, that that is precisely the same magnitude of reduction as was promised by the hon. member for St. John's West in his budget of December, 1979.
In addition, we look at the figures for the budgetary deficit. The budgetary deficit will decline from $14.2 billion in 198081 to $ 11.8 billion in 1983-84. Finally, as a percentage of gross national product, the deficit declines from being 5 per cent of gross national product in this fiscal year to being 2.9 per cent of of gross national product in 1983-84; nearly a 50 per cent reduction in the percentage share of gross national product that is represented by the deficit of the federal government. That is an achievement that we are projecting and we will be proud to see occur.

speechtext:
February 16, 1981
Borrowing Authority
I have always been a strong supporter of Canadianization, Mr. Speaker, but I take great exception to what the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance said and to the attitude of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde)-that money for acquisitions is no object as long as it is being coughed up by somebody else, that is, by the Canadian taxpayer. That is what the president of Petro-Canada said when he was asked where he would get the money from. He said that the Canadian taxpayer would shell out. What other attitude could explain authorizing Petro-Canada to buy out Petrofina at $120 a share-$59 above its trading value when this takeover was first rumoured? Nobody can make any sense-regardless of what the parliamentary secretary says-of a government which comes along and says that it will make an acquisition but will give a monetary gift of an additional $59 over and above what the shares were being traded for when it first began to think of acquiring Petrofina.
What really disturbs me about this is the priority accorded by this government to the manner in which it spends the Canadian taxpayers' money. It is willing to shell out a lot more money than it should to buy up an oil company. It is willing to send the money off to the vaults of some happy Belgians but it is not willing to do the things which should be done here at home.
It really disturbed me to learn that while the government was throwing money away on inflated shares and in other cases buying for Canadians what they already own, it is turning its back on the spending priorities which could bring about an equitable distribution of services for Canadians all across this country. The government is turning its back on the real needs of this country. That is what really concerns me. Its priorities are screwed up-there is no other way to put it.
Canadians have been really shaken in recent weeks to learn what little priority the government is giving to the development of trained research staff and innovative research programs in this country. Of course, it does pay lip service to research and development, but when it comes to supplying an adequate amount of government funds to the research granting councils of this country it falls woefully short of even the most basic requirements.
When the government goes abroad to borrow an additional $14 billion in foreign markets for heaven knows what-it does not explain that-it is backing away from the commitment which was made last year to carry out the five-year plan of adequate funding to the research granting councils. There are two important factors which we should bear in mind when we look at these councils in their role of furthering research and development in Canada. First, you must consider that a five-year plan is vitally necessary if scientists, engineers and medical researchers are to be properly trained and if the innovative research programs they undertake are to be carried through to conclusion. This cannot be a stop and go proposition. You cannot say to a researcher that funding will be available this year but next year it will be someone else's turn. People must be trained on an ongoing basis. You cannot say about a
research project, whatever the field of science, that the particular project can be developed for the next 12 months but then must be abandoned for the next couple of years in order to start up something else. That is not the way to carry research programs to conclusion. Scientific research just does not work in that way. There must be continuity and consistency. There must be an environment created which allows those involved to look beyond next month and next year to well into the future. That is the first point about the granting councils.
The second point is that it cannot be an on-again, off-again proposition, as I have said. We must also bear in mind that the research granting councils are the very engine which motivates the spark, the impetus for much of this scientific and technological research in Canada today. The research councils are really the granting agencies through which funding is channelled to train and produce the human plant, the human resources without which there can be no progress.
The Minister of State for Science and Technology and Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) can talk in grandiose terms about providing incentives to carry out more research and development. But industry knows full well that even if you have incentives coming out of your ears you cannot put them to good effect unless you have the highly trained scientific manpower and womanpower to take advantage of those incentives. You simply cannot do without the highly skilled human plant.
There is a lack of trained scientific and engineering personnel in Canada today, which is already beginning to have a serious impact on the Canadian economy. Thus, we have two options. We can import personnel from abroad, as we have done in the past, although I suggest that option is less open to us now than it was 15 or 20 years ago. That is one option. The second option is to train the personnel here in Canada. The latter course is obviously the course of wisdom. But in order to do this the government must comprehend and come to grips with the need for funding research granting councils on a long term basis.
These two points which I have mentioned interact. More than that, if properly implemented they will provide an essential ingredient to Canada's future prosperity. They will provide a highly trained force of scientists, engineers and medical researchers who will be the backbone of Canadian industry and, hence, Canadian employment in general.
The history of the struggle to achieve this laudable and obviously sensible goal has not been an easy one. I remind the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance just how difficult it was with the Liberal government throughout the 1970s. At that time it failed to realize the potential of the research granting councils. One might use the analogy that it kept them at starvation wages on a month to month basis. There was no comprehension as to how the granting councils could be the engine to generate greater industrial output or how they could initiate preventive medical programs which would reduce the vast sums of money which we must now spend on health and medical care. In fact, the councils were treated as just another suppliant coming to the Treasury Board
February 16, 1981

each year to be given their crumbs from the table. Their very existence throughout the decade of the 1970s was precarious. I have no doubt that there were Liberal cabinet ministers as, indeed, there were Liberal backbenchers who argued the case and the cause of the research granting councils. But their voices were weak and their political clout lacking. As a result, our talented personnel, our indigenous research projects and our industrial and medical development suffered through the 1970s.
I want to say, sir, that that changed when the Clark government came to office; a new approach was taken to the research granting councils. It says something about the differences in priority that we accorded to spending.
Adding to interest payments on borrowed moneys was not one of our priorities. Generating greater industrial development through improved research and technology was. And we knew where to start: with the research granting councils. I am sure I do not breach cabinet confidentiality when 1 say there were arguments in cabinet about the funding of the councils, but there were far more voices raised in favour of putting them on a proper financial footing than against, which is so different from the situation today.
The result of what was done under the Clark government was something in which I took pride. That result brought about a long-sought Conservative Party objective. It put the granting councils on a long-term, five-year basis so that they had adequate lead time for planning, and it dramatically increased their funding during the first year of that five-year plan.
Let us look at the record in comparison with what had gone before. The Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council had its budget increased by $41 million, or 35 per cent. The Social Sciences and Elumanities Research Council had its budget increased by $5.8 million, or 16.7 per cent. The Medical Research Council had its budget increased by $12.8 million, or 17.4 per cent. A 35 per cent increase for the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council was brought in by the Clark government. Compare that to the 12 per cent and 8 per cent increases that the former Liberal government had allocated to that council in 1978 and 1979. It was just enough to meet inflation but not enough to initiate innovative research programs.
What we have seen recently gives pause to what the present government's intention is and how different it is to the reaction accorded the former government's moves in this direction. The reaction of the scientific community to the Conservative government's recognition of the importance of the granting councils was immediate, and, needless to say, positive. It had been given an infusion, a new lease on life. Plans were developed which would be ongoing; projects were undertaken which would be assured of a more than one year lifespan; and, most important, the numbers of young people engaged in scientific and medical research training were greatly expanded. The
Borrowing Authority
engine was rolling and the end result for Canada would be highly beneficial.
That was the situation a year ago. What do we find one year later with another Liberal government back in office? We find a minister struggling valiantly, I have no doubt, to maintain the program the Conservative Party initiated, but a minister with little clout and little support in cabinet. And as he battles away in a cabinet that is devoting most of its time and energy to borrowing moneys for less worth-while objectives, word is spreading throughout Canada's scientific community that it has been sold out.
I quote from an article on page 15 of the Ottawa Citizen, February 6, 1981, as follows:
In what scientists consider the ultimate doublecross, the federal government has scuttled a major program for revitalization of university research and scientific training programs.
The article goes on to state:
Designed to get Canadian researchers back to work and offset severe shortages of young engineers and scientists, the plan called for significant budget increases for the council until 1985. Despite reassurances the five-year plan would continue this year, however, it has been quietly sabotaged.
I should like to put on record what one member of the scientific community wrote to me from Kingston when he learned about the plans of the Liberal government to scuttle the five-year plan and lower funding to the research councils. As he contemplated the government's reneging on the five-year plan of assistance and the effect on the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council, he wrote:
We simply cannot start and stop five-year plans in this stupid way. In the case of NSERC this means that various new programs started in 1980-81 will cither have to be closed down or seriously curtailed after but one year of operation. Specifically:
1.	The University Research Fellowship Program has already been curtailed from 100 positions per year to only 75 for 1981 -82;
2.	The budget for replacement of worn out and obsolete equipment has been slashed by many millions of dollars;
3.	The new program of undergraduate summer research awards (to encourage undergraduate students to prepare for careers in research and development) must be in some jeopardy;
4.	The project research applicable in industry (PRAI) grant scheme, a very effective way of bringing industries and universities together will be seriously diminished in impact.
He is analysing the effect on the research community of what this government has done in cutting back, year after year, worth-while programs which had been initiated and worth-while programs and long-term research funding which would involve newly trained people in Canada-good doctors, geophysicists, chemists, electronic engineers, mechanical scientists, all of whom are involved in this new program and who take time to train. If the money is not available to finance that training period, then it is we in Canada who will not have enough men and women to staff our hospitals, search for our oil, test our drugs, modernize our computers, design our engines or improve our nuclear power.
This is what the government's program is doing at the present time. As the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance so proudly pointed out, the government has decided to take a great amount of money and send it abroad to pay for

February 16, 1981
Borrowing Authority
inflated shares of the newly-acquired Petrofina. It will take that out of Canadian taxpayers' money and be willing to spend it abroad on something that will not benefit Canadians, but it will not continue the funding to the granting councils at the same level as last year, funding that is so necessary if we are to have the kind of industrial development that this country is crying out for.
That is why I say the government has its priorities all screwed up. That is why I say the kind of gibberish we heard from the parliamentary secretary earlier today does not make any sense when worth-while programs are being slashed in order to feed the ego of some particular minister, be it the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. As I was saying when I was very rudely interrupted, the hon. member knows the reasons behind this undertaking of Canadian governments.

I would like to point out at least one misconception the member has about the current white paper. Fie called peacekeeping the last priority in that white paper. Where did he get that notion? Certainly not from the white paper itself. I quote from the 1971 white paper as follows:
The policy announced by the Prime Minister on April 3, 1969, initiated the process of adjusting the balance between Canadian defence activities to ensure that priorities for defence were responsive to national interests and international developments.
A process of adjusting which is responsive to national interests and international developments is found in the white paper. To me this portrays an evolution which has taken place and continues to take place so that the basis of the white paper remains as valid today as it was ten years ago. Reading on in the white paper we find:
Four major areas of ativity for the Canadian forces were identified in summary form as follows:
(a)	the surveillance of our own territory and coastlines, i.e. the protection of
our sovereignty;
(b)	the defence of North America in co-operation with U.S. forces;

time to time assume.
This paper will next examine these four areas of defence policy in detail.
Nowhere, so far, have these four areas of defence policy been called priorities in either descending or ascending order. Perhaps the member from Victoria would like to examine the white paper again.

At this point in the white paper we find that activity in each area must be assessed in terms of the priorities which have been, and if I may add, continue to be established.
The four areas of defence policy remain as eminently viable today as they were ten years ago, but the priority assigned to each is the subject of an evolutionary process which continues to take place. Instead of encouraging further efforts for the defence of Canada, the hon. member opposite has preferred to take cheap shots at the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence. For some reason, perhaps because he was frustrated by his own inability to persuade his cabinet colleagues in the previous Conservative government to achieve greater defence aims, he has chosen in his speech to denigrate government efforts to upgrade our defence capabilities.
The hon. member may prefer to speak of the past rather than the present or the future, but since this government took office we have achieved a great deal in national defence of which we are justifiably proud. We have chosen a new fighter aircraft which will enable our air force to carry out our commitments at home and abroad, and in so doing we have negotiated an excellent contract which is bringing considerable industrial benefits to this country. We are forging ahead with our plans to provide the navy with six new frigates while at the same time enhancing our Canadian naval shipbuilding capability. We have taken the means to extend the life of 16 of our existing 19 destroyers to maintain our naval capability until new frigates enter service.
After receiving new Leopard tanks, the army is taking delivery of 441 new armoured vehicles and a variety of wheeled vehicles of all types. We will soon be letting a contract for 2,800 new 2!/2-ton trucks. Plans also call for the purchase of 2,500 new jeeps in the near future.
We have initiated a search and rescue capability update program and we have earmarked more resources to be provided to reserves as equipment for their training, including helicopters and armoured vehicles.
Delivery of all 18 Aurora long-range patrol aircraft will soon be completed, on time and on budget. I need not remind the hon. member of the highly unfounded criticism of the opposition when we launched that program, one which has proven very successful despite the political play he and his colleagues made at the time.

speechtext: I have heard the hon. member. This appears to be a debate between two hon. members. With the consent of the House, I would prefer to recognize now the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke).

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on Bill C-59, the borrowing authority bill, once again; that is to say, in another year and not another time on the same bill. I am impressed with the simplicity of the bill. It is smaller than most which we get a chance to debate here. There is only one clause other than the title. One wonders why we are spending so much time of the House on such a small bill, one that must be fairly straightforward. In fact, one might wonder why we are spending so much time on this bill regarding which the government has once again seen fit to invoke closure. This is the third time in five months that we have had closure invoked to stop the voices of the opposition from speaking out on matters of importance to Canadian taxpayers. After having taken an absolutely irresponsible attitude and invoked closure, the government then starts putting up speakers one for one, matching the speakers on the opposition side.
The hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) used his full allotted time. Your Honour interrupted him at the end of his time. The hon. member for York South-Weston (Mrs. Appolloni) just gave a speech which I suggest belonged to some other debate. I do not recall her mentioning much, if anything, to do with this bill. It is bad enough that the government uses this further muzzle on the opposition by putting up speaker for speaker, but the last two government speakers have been parliamentary secretaries. For the executive on the other side to be chewing up opposition time in a way like that is unpalatable and disgusting.
Offensive.

Yes, offensive. There are two main reasons why this bill is so important, deserves a long debate and should not be cut off by this closure move. The first is the size of the authority sought by this bill, $14 billion. The second is the underlying ills that have produced the deficits which have made this amount of borrowing necessary.
There used to be an infamous saying attributed to the Grits-"What's a million?" Now we can ask ourselves in the same tone whether they have adjusted that to "What's a billion?"
When I go around my constituency, I give explanations to various school classes. From time to time I explain what is a billion. I am beginning to wonder if I have been explaining to the wrong people. Maybe I should make some of those explanations here. It is the government opposite which has a greater need to know what is a billion.
I could give an example here. Probably many members buy lottery tickets. I will take the case of a Canadian who wins $1 million dollars in the lottery. He invests that $1 million dollars
February !6, 1981

at 10 per cent. I just use that percentage for ease of figuring, because with the inflationary rates of interest that this government has given us, he would get a lot more than that; but 10 per cent is an easy figure to get, and it is an easy figure to use. He would have an income of $100,000 a year, and that is, roughly speaking, $2,000 a week. Well, I suppose we all know somebody in the neighbourhood that earns $2,000 a week or $100,000 a year. But if we gave that same lottery winner $1 billion and he invested it in the same way, he would have an income of $100 million a year, or $2 million a week, and 1 do not think any of us could say we know anybody that had an income of that magnitude. It is about time that the government started thinking in billions instead of in millions.
Another example is a stack of bills. If we take a stack of $1,000 bills and we have a thousand of them, that will give us a stack of paper eight inches high. It does not take too much arithmetic to realize that if you multiply that stack of $1,000 bills by a thousand to get to $1 billion, you would have a stack of bills that was 667 feet tall. I am sorry I do not have the metric measurement. But if you stop and think of that size of stack of bills, that is a stack of bills higher than the length of two football fields. There is quite a difference between an eight-inch stack to make $1 million and a 667-foot stack to make $1 billion.
The final example that I often use is if we go back to the first year of our Lord and an individual had obtained $1 billion at that time, in A.D. 0, in other words, or A.D. 1, however you want to count it, and had started spending that money just straight off the top, no interest at all, in the year 1981, after spending $1,000 a day, for nearly 2,000 years that individual would still have $277 million left. He would be good for a lot more time spending $1,000 a day, and this is without receiving any interest, which I think is an important thing to remember.
Maybe this government is now finding out what a billion is worth, because their policy agent, Mr. Hopper, the president of Petro-Canada, has come crying back to the trough. He says, "But fellas, you know, I've bought that company you wanted me to buy, but now I need $1.5 billion, because my treasury is empty and 1 have not got the money in my coffers. So I want you guys to get the money somewhere. Maybe you will tax the consumers of gasoline or petroleum products, or maybe just go back to the printing press and print some more money." I do not think Mr. Hopper is telling us where to get it, but he needs $1.46 billion to complete the purchase of Petrofina. I would have thought that this outfit across there would have thought about it before asking Mr. Hopper, with his bankrupt or, at least, insolvent company, to buy that other company for them.
How is the government going to raise this $1.46 billion, and what is it going to cost? If, as Mr. Hopper suggests, the government just taxes Canadians to raise it, it will cost $65 per capita. Each and every person will have to pay $65. Well, that does not sound too bad; but if you take an average family of five, which is having a tough enough time as it is, then that family has to raise $325 in order to pay for the new toy,

Petrofina, of the government. Well, maybe $325 is not so bad either; but we have to relate this $1.46 billion to the total debt of this government that they have run up over the years. It is hard to figure out exactly what the national debt is these days, but the public accounts, which I brought along today, indicate that the liabilities of the Government of Canada are $106 billion as at the end of the last fiscal period.
If we apply some simple arithmetic to that, it develops that that debt will apply to every Canadian, at the rate of $4,425. That is in addition to the other and ordinary personal borrowings that individuals make in Canada to acquire automobiles or homes or whatever they borrow money for. Again, if I apply that $4,425 per capita to the average family of five, it comes out to well over $20,000 for that family in addition to anything else it may have borrowed.
What exactly is $14 billion, and how much is that in relation to whatever else we have? It is about 14 per cent of the total liabilities that we have already. I consulted the taxation statistics, the 1980 edition, which is the latest one out, which analyses returns of individuals for the 1978 taxation year. Summary table two in that book shows that in 1978 $14 billion was the amount of federal tax collected from 14 million individuals who filed income tax returns that year. What this government is asking us to do by Bill C-59 is to take an amount equal to the total amount of tax paid by all individual taxpayers in this country two years ago, and just add it on, because they need some more money, to the total debt that these poor taxpayers are already saddled with.
The long-term policies which have resulted in this kind of situation developing where we need this borrowing bill are just that: long-term policies. They are not something that has popped up to surprise the government, and I have already referred to having had these borrowing bills before. Again, I refer to the 1980 public accounts. In the last five fiscal years, that is, from 1976 to 1980, the deficits incurred by the government have totalled $49 billion. Of course, not all of that is cash, but the cash requirements over that same five-year period were $40 billion. During that same five-year period, the unmatured debt, which I will have something to say about a little further on, increased by $34 billion. The total debt of the government is unknown. It is not known, probably, by anyone. Again referring to public accounts, page 2.9 in the current volume, the statement of assets and liabilities of the government shows liabilities, other than those for annuities, insurance and pensions, of $83 billion. Now, that is not quite the $106 billion of the total liabilities. In that same report, we can find liabilities of Crown corporations which are not consolidated, but are debts guaranteed by the government and have to be added, and that is another $8 billion. Those all bear interest. The contingent liabilities, which do not bear interest yet, are shown there as $4 billion. We also have unrecorded liabilities. These are arising mostly from pension indexing for those civil servants who are already retired, and also from termination benefits for those who are about to retire.

As hon. members well know, the public accounts are full of gems of information for those who are willing to dig for them and study them. I found a write-off in fiscal year 1979 of $546 million because of adjustments of assets for values. Then in 1980, the last fiscal year, $1.5 billion was written off, again to adjust the accounts to their proper values.
Earlier this month the public accounts committee was told by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited to expect a write-off of about $700 million. Atomic Energy of Canada Limited was not quite sure of the amount which had resulted from La Prade and two other heavy water plants built by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited having to be closed down because there was no market for their products. What I am saying is that there is much debt shown in the public accounts, and the $100 billion figure I used can be well established.
Having established the size of the debt to some measure, we then have to determine the cost of borrowing all this money. Again I refer to the public accounts, which show a total unmatured debt of $72 billion at an average interest rate in 1980 of 10.13 per cent. It might be worth noting at this point that the government too is suffering from its inflationary policies in that only five years ago, in 1976, the government was borrowing at a rate below 8 per cent. The present rate of 10.13 per cent is up 29 per cent over 1976.
They are not borrowing at 10 per cent any more.

Goodness knows what the government will be paying. That will be disclosed in the next public accounts. The rate will probably be closer to 12 per cent. I want to remind hon. members, and particularly members of the Grit government, that the government used to have the ability to borrow at 3 per cent because that was about what the real value of renting money or borrowing money was. However, with inflationary policies-most notably put into effect over the past six to eight years-interest rates have risen to such a level because they must reflect the rate of inflation plus the natural worth of the money, which would be about 3 per cent.
What does the total direct borrowing cost us? It is easy to see that if we applied the 10.13 per cent to the $72 billion reported as unmatured direct debt, that comes to an interest cost of well over $7 billion. That is each and every year. We have heard that it will continue to rise, but using the $7.3 billion, how does that compare as an interest cost with other costs and transactions of the government? The total 1980 expenditures, again in the public accounts, were $51 billion, so we can see that $7.3 billion works out to 14 cents out of every dollar the government spends being used to pay interest on debt.
That is serious enough, but if we compare that cost with revenues, we find that of the total tax revenues in 1980 of $35 billion, the $7 billion means that 21 cents out of every dollar the government takes in in tax revenues goes out right away to pay interest on this debt.
If we want to shock taxpayers in a real way, we can go back to those taxpayers I spoke of earlier who, in 1978, paid $14 billion in tax. We can see that over half of all the individual income tax paid in 1978 went toward covering the interest costs of this government. Comparing that figure with 1980 when personal tax revenues increased, as most taxpayers know from looking in their pocketbooks, we find that the rate was 43 cents. That means that 43 cents out of every dollar every individual Canadian taxpayer paid to this government went to cover interest on debt.
Perhaps that is enough of looking back. I have established what the costs are and where the borrowings of the government are at this point. Perhaps we should look ahead a little and see what will happen and what we can look forward to with this government. After all, it was not many months ago- April 14, 1980-when the throne speech produced by the government opposite announced the following:
It is the intention of my government to continue the policies of expenditure restraint-
We can all have a laugh at that.
-and improved government administration ... Improving the efficiency of the federal government is as important an objective of these reforms as reducing the deficit.
Following the example of the Progressive Conservative government in the Thirty-first Parliament, 1 see that the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), in presenting his budget last year did a Five-year forward projection. It is interesting that that was the first time any Liberal government had ever seen fit to do that. He was following the example of the former minister of finance, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), who became the first finance minister ever to make a five-year forward projection.
What do this government's projections show? First of all, in addition to the $51 billion I spoke of which we are spending in the 1980 Fiscal year, the increases are shown at 15 per cent, then the next year at 12 per cent, the following year at 11 per cent and finally, for 1984, another 11 per cent increase. These are cumulative increases which will result in expenditures by the 1984 fiscal period of $81 billion. We have to find another $30 billion to spend and, knowing the government opposite, it will probably want to borrow again when that time comes.
In addition to the increases in expenditures the same table shows increases in deficits. There will be another $63 billion added on to the total deficits of this government since confederation and an increase in borrowings will be necessary. Further borrowings of $39 billion will be needed during the next four years.
With more borrowing and the higher interest rates about which my friend, the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), was just telling us, it is not hard to imagine what kind of difficulty we will have in relation to the portions of budgets which will be taken up by the interest load this government has put upon us.
Do the Grits opposite know what is happening? I rather suspect they do not. Again I refer to comments offered by the Auditor General in his 1979 annual report wherein he made a
