speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of convening a federal-provincial meeting at the earliest date possible for the establishment of a national power grid that would connect all power systems in Canada and also, where possible, effect connections with grid systems in the United States, thus fully utilizing the power potential that exists in Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is not a new topic. It has been discussed in this Flouse on many occasions but it is one that is most appropriate at this particular stage in our country's history. It is appropriate because, while we spend a great deal of time talking about oil and gas, there are many other forms of power which are of significance to the future development of our nation.
While these days we hear a great deal about the possibility of a major power shift from central Canada to the west, there is, in my opinion, as great a potential, if not greater, for the same type of power shift occurring in eastern Canada or in the Atlantic provinces, depending on where you come from. In the west they think that eastern Canada is Ontario and Quebec; in the maritimes or in the Atlantic provinces we think eastern Canada is the Atlantic provinces. But it is one of the sad facts of life and of history that as far back as 1959 we were very close to achieving a federal-provincial agreement-on which the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) will elaborate in the very near future-which could
National Power Grid
have put in place a national power grid and eliminated, to a very significant degree, the insecurity of resource supplies in the fields of energy which exist at present and have put the Atlantic provinces and all of eastern Canada in the position of having to rely far too often upon the whims of the oil barons of the world.
To outline in a little detail some of the benefits which would come to the whole nation from the development of a national power grid, let me state some of the potentials which exist in Atlantic Canada and which are ours for development if a national power grid is put in place. We know about the problems between Newfoundland and Labrador and the province of Quebec so far as Churchill Falls is concerned. We know of the tremendous power potential which is associated with Churchill Falls and the development which has occurred there since the harnessing of Churchill Falls by Brinco. But we also hear a great deal in this House and other places about the possibilities of the Lower Churchill and the frustrations faced by the people in Newfoundland and Labrador over the fact that they cannot develop this tremendous power resource which they see there, both because of the transmission system which at this time will only move that power through the province of Quebec and because of a long-term agreement which was worked out between the then premier of Newfoundland, Joey Smallwood, and the government of Quebec many, many years ago, which, unfortunately for Newfoundland and Labrador, is to apply for many years in the future.
Let us stop to think what would happen if we had a national power grid and the opportunity to lay a cable which would move that power in Newfoundland and Labrador through Newfoundland to Cape Breton Island and on to Nova Scotia, and which would pick up the resources which are ours in the coal fields of Cape Breton, not to mention the coal fields on the mainland of Nova Scotia. Certainly the coal fields of Cape Breton are harnessed to a significant degree by the Buchanan government. This would offset the tremendous dependence which we have at present on bunker C oil which comes from off our shores and, unfortunately, in many instances from Arab nations, upon which we cannot depend because they themselves cannot depend on their capability to produce and deliver the oil which is theirs to sell.
However, let us go a little farther, past Cape Breton and the oil there to the Bay of Fundy and the tremendous possibilities which are associated with power generation there. Only last week I attended meetings in New York City with Premier John Buchanan and other experts associated with tidal power in Nova Scotia at which we talked with the New York State Power Authority and other people in the state about Fundy tidal power and its development.
As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, we in Nova Scotia have under way at this time a pilot project on the development of tidal power at the Annapolis River. That project will be completed in 1983 when, for the first time, a new type of generator called a straight-flow generator will be used for the harnessing of the waters in the Bay of Fundy which are at the Annapolis River to see if that particular generator will work as

February 16, 1981
National Power Grid
effectively as its creators believe it will. If it does, then it will be used onwards to the Minas Basin where the hydro power which could be produced is almost beyond man's comprehension. It would certainly be of the magnitude of Niagara Falls, if certain sites were chosen in the Minas Basin to develop that power. It would be comparable to James Bay in Quebec as a potential source of power.
What we require, even if we are going to harness the tides of the Bay of Fundy, are transmission lines which would deliver the power in question to users who require it at this time. There is no doubt about the fact that a national power grid, if it were developed, would guarantee that the power would be made available first to Canadians, that they would have the first opportunity to take advantage of the tremendous power potential available in those Fundy tides. But even if that could not happen overnight with the construction of transmission lines, either through New Brunswick to the New England grid or under water through the Bay of Fundy to Maine, we could still put that power into an area which could immediately use it. It would assist in the payment for the actual barrages which would have to be constructed and the generation systems which would have to be put in place, as well as the cost of transmission lines which would be required to deliver power to the area where it is needed at present. With payment, you could have a system whereby there would be a diminishing supply of that power going outside our nation if it were required in our nation, and if we had a national power grid in place we would be able to deliver that power to whichever part of this nation required it. That is what is so important about a national power grid. That is the difference between what we have now and what we should have had yesterday.
The tremendous advantage is that hydro, whether it be from tidal power or from rivers, gives two guarantees to the people of this nation. First, it gives pollution-free power. It does not run the risk of acid rain, nor the risk of destroying the environment, as does open strip mining and things of that nature. None of those problems is involved. Second, it provides inflation-free power. Once the dams are built, for instance the ones associated with Churchill Falls, the Lower Churchill or Fundy tidal power, they are in place for 50 to 75 years. Over that period of time the cost of the power would be a known fact, with very little escalation of any kind.
With regard to Fundy tidal power, the tides come in and the tides go out. Price does not make any difference because the tides still come in and go out. Once the dams are built they are in place, and it has been suggested that they would be in place for 75 years. This indicates that we will know the cost of that power today and, really, 75 years from now. The experts say that there is less than a 1 per cent inflation factor associated with the development of that kind of power. It is a substantial difference, especially when one looks at oil which was $2 per barrel in 1973 and today is something like $36 U.S. per barrel, with many experts saying that the price of oil will soon be something like $100 U.S. per barrel.
When one looks at those figures and the possible development in eastern Canada, one has some appreciation of what could be done if we could only develop a national power grid as soon as possible. As the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain will point out in detail, much of it is in place now, It is simply a matter of developing the connectors and upgrading the transmission lines across the country so that we can move power back and forth where it is needed.
These days we talk a great deal about security of supply for oil and gas. We in eastern Canada know of our potential to participate in making a two-way pipeline for either oil or gas tremendously valuable to the whole nation from a security of supply point of view. We can look at a national power grid in exactly the same manner. With such a power grid we could give a guaranteed security of supply not only to eastern Canada but to the entire nation from the point of view of being able to move electrical energy from Labrador to British Columbia. That is what the country requires; that is the foresight our leaders must have. It is the reason I suggest that there should be a federal-provincial conference committed to the development of an agreement which will ensure that this moves forward.
I suggest that agreement does not have to be at the first minister's level in the beginning. I believe we have resource ministers across the country with the foresight to want the required interconnections to ensure that we have a national power grid. It saddens me that although since 1973 we have been told the facts of life as far as oil supplies in the world and in this country are concerned, we have not moved or we have moved like turtles when we should have run like deer. Even at this late stage we must see to it that a mechanism is put in place which can produce a national power grid to move electricity, not only back and forth across the nation but north and south when it is required, and in many instances it is.
With power in the maritimes, with Fundy tidal power in Nova Scotia, certainly we will need to connect with American power systems to move our power north and south, to pay for the required facilities, to retain the long-term benefits for Canadians, and in the short term meet the problems faced by our American friends who are also in the same box as far as security of supply for energy needs are concerned, especially oil. They are most anxious to get out of oil usage and turn to alternate sources of energy, so that they will have a security of supply the same as we in eastern Canada desire.
As this debate goes on, I hope a determination will be expressed by the House to ensure that some initiatives are taken at the federal level to put in place, as quickly as possible, a national power grid for the benefit of all Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roy MacLaren (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL POWER GRID
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion this afternoon by the hon. member opposite was introduced against the background of the recent National Energy Program announced by the government. It is within that context that I want to say a word about the motion and then turn to the more specific questions of the hon. member concerning the
February 16, 1981

possibilities of a national energy grid, and also his concluding point with regard to electricity exports to the United States.
The House may recall that it was noted in the National Energy Program that Canada's capacity in electricity has more than kept pace with our demand for electricity, and that that margin of capacity gives us an opportunity to analyse further the choices we shall have to make regarding the generation of electricity in the future.
In referring to that element of the National Energy Program, the hon. member understandably concentrated on the requirements, as he sees them, of the region from which he comes. Indeed, electricity is a source of energy which holds great promise in the maritime provinces of Canada.
The National Energy Program draws attention to the opportunities represented by a number of major projects in the Atlantic provinces to which the hon. member referred. I am speaking of the Lower Churchill project which is under active consideration at the moment. Certainly it is the government's view, as indicated in the National Energy Program, that the technical, financial and political barriers to the rapid development of Lower Churchill power must be overcome without delay. In addition to that commitment, the National Energy Program and, indeed, existing initiatives of the federal government are also directed toward the generation of electricity in the Atlantic provinces in such novel ways as the tidal power to which the hon. member opposite referred. He will be aware of the federal financing of a development project in that regard, a project which I am sure all members in the House hope will indicate a viable and prosperous future for that particular potential source of electrical power.
Beyond that, of course, the member is conscious, as I am sure we all are, of the need to ensure alternative energy sources to that of oil-fired electricity generation in the Atlantic provinces. Therefore, the emphasis in the program is also on environmentally acceptable conversions to coal of oil-fired capacity in electricity generating stations, where that opportunity exists.
Against that background of electricity generation potential in the maritime provinces-and I have touched upon only one or two examples-I want to say a word about a national power grid to which the hon. member opposite has drawn the attention of the House. That question is not a new one by any means. As the hon. member pointed out, it is not a new idea. It has been discussed over the past decades, and there has been a continuing interest in that time in the possibilities offered by a national power grid.
There have been two major studies undertaken on an interprovincial basis to explore the opportunities for strengthening the electrical connections between provinces. The first of those studies began in 1962, almost 20 years ago. It was completed in two stages under the direction of a federal-provincial working group on long distance electricity transmission. At that time the committee had to indicate the nature and extension of the potential benefits of a trans-Canada interconnection as its
National Power Grid
objective, which might be expected to bring significant benefits to the whole Canadian economy. A further major expectation was that the grid would reduce the need for investment in generating capacity and, additionally, would reduce operating costs. The first stage of that study was completed in 1963. It was followed by a more detailed investigation.
The result of the study stated that there would be savings. But they were seen as minor savings-less than 1 per cent of the total electricity system investment. At that time the committee findings indicated that to obtain the maximum benefit of a national development plant would require the full co-ordination, planning, development and operation of the interconnected utilities. Of course, in turn, that implied a requirement for some form of central planning and operating authority. The members of the committee concluded that the estimated net benefits of the national network were too limited to justify the further immediate development of the idea. However, the committee did recommend that the subject be re-examined at a later date.
Some years later, in 1977, the possibility of a type of interprovincial grid was, indeed, examined by an interprovincial advisory committee on energy. A study group was established which undertook an assessment in a somewhat similar manner to the earlier study to which I have referred. In October, 1978, a report was issued which concluded that there was a very modest, but positive, indication that the value of strengthened east-west interconnections in the electricity system of Canada would increase over time.
From that very brief and somewhat simplified view of the studies, it can be seen that there were some indications of benefit from a major expansion of regional interconnections. Those benefits were seen as small, in terms of the total investment which would be required in the electricity industry in the years ahead. It was also seen that in order to achieve such modest benefits some form of central planning would be required. There were indications that the provinces would see this as an unacceptable limitation of their flexibility in their own planning of electricity capacity.
On the other hand, it is evident that there has been progress among electrical utilities in Canada in co-operating among themselves. Certainly, on occasion the national government has acted to encourage them to do so. For example, from the two studies to which I have referred, the provinces became more active in expanding their regional connections.
When the federal-provincial committee began its work in 1963, the major north-south transmission system between the Peace River hydro development in northern British Columbia, to take an example, and the load centres in the southern part of the province had not been completed. The Nelson River system in Manitoba had not been committed. The eastern-western portions of the Ontario system were isolated, as were the eastern-western parts of the Quebec hydro system. At that time no transmission interconnections existed between Quebec and Labrador or between Quebec and New Brunswick. Prince Edward Island was isolated from the mainland. The results of the studies encouraged an increased growth of transmission

February 16, 1981
National Power Grid
lines in many of the provinces. The federal government played an important role in assisting the provinces in the development of their electrical generation capacity and transmission facilities.
1 would like to give one or two examples of such federal involvement. They include the extensive support of provincial electrical research and development, such as the $25 million contribution to the demonstration of low head hydro power at Annapolis, Nova Scotia, to which the hon. member made reference. This was a commitment to provide a loan of up to almost $200 million at Crown corporation rates. To date, over $100 million has been spent for transmission facilities from the Nelson River development in Manitoba. Other participation by the federal government was demonstrated in the joint involvement with the Newfoundland government to study the hydro potential of the Lower Churchill Falls in Labrador from which there are high expectations of real benefit. The federal government has also assisted in the construction of the cable between the mainland and Prince Edward Island, which substantially reduced the cost of electricity generation in that province.
It is obvious from these and other elements that in the past the federal government has been active in assisting the provinces to develop efficient and effective hydroelectric and other electrical capacity. Not only has the federal government demonstrated its interest and concern in the past but it is committed to playing an important role in the future.
To sustain Canada's energy security in the long run we need to substitute more plentiful forms of energy for those forms which are now less plentiful and more expensive, particularly oil. Within that program, as I have already noted, electricity remains a major element.
To that end the government has embarked upon a program to encourage Canadians to convert their domestic heating from oil to natural gas in some areas and to electricity in others. The incentive program, Canadians will want to recognize, does include electricity just as much as it does oil.
If our goal of substitution were achieved tomorrow, that is, the goal of reducing our use of oil in residential, commercial and industrial sectors to 10 per cent of the total energy used in those sectors, the daily saving would be almost 400,000 barrels of oil, the equivalent of what we import today.
The National Energy Program looks toward the ecourage-ment in the Atlantic provinces in particular of the substitution of electricity, where practical, for the high cost and limited oil that is available. That program will begin to be implemented vigorously in the months immediately ahead.
In addition to discussing some of the domestic benefits of electricity co-operation among provinces which in the hon. member's view would best take the form of a national electricity grid, I want to touch on the international aspect the hon. member raised, and that is a power grid which would maximize connections with the United States. In that regard hon. members may recall that international trade in electricity has
grown dramatically in recent years; since 1975 there has been nearly a fivefold increase in our net exports. Net revenues from the export of electricity have risen from approximately $1 million in 1975 to almost $7.5 million in 1979. In fact, in 1979 our net export of electricity represented 9 per cent of net Canadian electricity generation.
Such a growing level of electricity exports understandably raises the question of whether the interconnections between the Canadian and the United States facilities are interfering with the development of greater regional interconnection within Canada.
I think it is worth taking a moment to explore some of the reasons for the growth in international links to determine whether there is any negative effect to the national interest or whether such exports represent a clear benefit to Canada and an activity which should be promoted and developed further.
During the early years of this century several hydroelectric developments were constructed in Canada, primarily to meet the needs of the neighbouring states of the United States. Some of those developments were undertaken under contract which continued up to as much as 60 years. That, in turn, led to some concern that the more attractive hydro sites were somehow being directed away from supplying the needs of the Canadian consumer. The isolated nature of electricity systems in the first decade of this century made it very difficult to replace energy from United States sources in the event that Canada wished to recapture its hydroelectric output. The export of electricity was actively discouraged by a number of measures and exports were regulated as early as 1907. From the period 1925 through 1963 a tax was levied on electricity exports, a fact that was not always recalled during the recent debate about taxes on the export of petroleum.
The establishment of the National Energy Board in 1959 provided an opportunity to review export applications in a much more comprehensive manner and to distinguish between export opportunities that could provide substantial benefit to Canadian customers from those that might endanger the cost of security of supply to Canadians.
More recently, the National Energy Board has put tests in place to ensure that exports will be permitted only after the Canadian people are assured of their own electricity requirements while at the same time taking the opportunities for foreign exchange earnings which such exports represent.
I do not doubt that in the time ahead we will hear more about the possibilities of electricity generation partly, perhaps, from the stations in the maritime provinces. It is an area to which the government is sensitive. We will work to assure the Canadian people that while their needs for electricity are fully met, equally the possibilities for co-operation with the United States in this area are also actively supported.
I touched upon some of the questions raised by the hon. member in his interesting statement. I think he will see that a number of initiatives have been taken in the past to encourage co-operation among the provinces in their electrical generation
February 16, 1981

activities. He will see there are aspects of the National Energy Program which are designed to encourage the further development of electricity capacity in the maritime provinces.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I am sure he will recognize that as a result of initiatives taken both by provincial governments and the federal government, the potential for electricity exports will be seriously examined and further developed as the capacity and needs of Canadians are met.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL POWER GRID
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we talk of a national policy for Canada, I do not think there is any debate or argument about the fact that the key component of any national energy program has to be an energy power grid which will carry power from all types of sources.
The parliamentary secretary has just finished outlining the sad story of inactivity on this proposal for 20 years. Let me refresh the memory of the House about things done a generation ago when we finished 22 years of inactivity on the part of the federal Parliament in regard to the development of Canada.
In 1957 a fresh new government came in with the national power grid in its policy resolutions from the 1956 convention. It went to work on the proposal with vigour, spoke to every provincial government, got the support of every provincial government, spoke to all the hydro commissions, power authorities private and public, got their support and in 1959, after the preliminary technical study, the prime minister of the day announced in Kitimat a national power grid for Canada.
This grid would not just carry the power from the hydro resources of Canada which were and are abundant, energy would come from many sources-the tar sands of Athabasca, the heavy oils of eastern Alberta the geothermal energy below the surface of all Saskatchewan and the resources of the prairies. It would take in coal, although we did not know the full amount there was in B.C., Alberta and Saskatchewan. In just those three provinces alone we now know there is over 200 billion tons of coal. We were looking to the coal of the offshore area because that figure of 250 billion tons I quoted does not apply to the northern parts of Canada, the Arctic Islands or the coal of the offshore area. That has a tremendous potential along the eastern part of the country. The Fundy Tidal Power was certainly part of that concept.
We visualize the power grid which runs from the Yukon in the north, with all the unused power each year going into the sea, together with all the power from the rivers in northeastern B.C., including the Peace River, the power from the Columbia system, the Saskatchewan Nelson system and the power from the Churchill. Then there is a big gap in northern Ontario. We thought of harnessing what is now called the James Bay power, the great power of the Churchill River and the tremendous offshore energy potential of the Atlantic provinces and bringing all of that and all of the LPP fuels for the fixed power part of the package. It was a great concept, but we had to
National Power Grid
assure ourselves that not only was it a hypothetical dream, it was an economically viable project. Even using the distressed prices of oil and gas referred to by the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester (Mr. Coates) that you could get offshore as dumped products, even referring to the very cheap power rates in Manitoba, what you will get in B.C., what you had in Ontario and what you were going to get in Quebec- with that, even as the parliamentary secretary stated, when that study was completed on the economic aspects as well as the physical and technical aspects the report in 1963 showed a marginal advantage. That was the case even at the low prices of that day.
What the parliamentary secretary forgot to tell you, Mr. Speaker, and Canadians, was that we went to that power grid as a basic fundamental in our national development policy because we knew from the Paley report in 1952 and the Netschert in 1959, and so on in that the world would be short of oil, the most popular form of energy in 1950. We knew that 1980 was the critical period and we had to get ready for that critical period. Prices would obviously have to rise from those rock bottom prices of $2 per barrel. If you were to add in the present costs of all the energy sources I have mentioned and put into that 1963 study what the benefit-cost ratio would be, as the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester said, it would be hard to grasp. Things are 30 times higher. Think what it would mean today to the Atlantic provinces if they were part of a national power grid, both contributing to and taking from that power grid. Think what it would mean to the hard-pressed industries of Ontario to get access to sure energy supplies, maybe coming from Alberta's coal or from Saskatchewan; maybe coming from as far away as the Yukon? The trick was bumping it back and forth.
As the parliamentary secretary mentioned, that report was never published. That report came into the hands of the minister in September, 1963. However, some of the information in it was obtained by talking to power corporations and commissions across the country. Some were private power corporations and did not want their figures known. When I asked the minister for a summary of the report, just to state what the parliamentary secretary stated here today, that the benefit cost was plus, we could not get it. From 1963 the provinces were forced, one by one, to develop their connections. They had already done it in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick in 1957 through the Atlantic Provinces Power Development Act, which was passed in this House to help those provinces build connections. Manitoba, Ontario, Saskatchewan, Alberta and B.C. are all being forced into the connection. Over the years they have developed the capacity to carry a higher voltage and reduce the cost.
Another factor is the research which has gone on. Take a look at what Quebec Hydro has done in research of high voltage transmission. What about the work done by the National Research Council, and what about the wind tunnel at the airport? What about that 1963 report and the losses that would not have to occur with our modern technology. That technology by Quebec Hydro and the National Research

February 16. 1981
National Power Grid
Council was available publicly 12 years ago, and nothing was done about it. The whole history of this subject, over the past 20 years has been sad. I cannot honestly blame anyone. There is this lethargy in Ottawa about doing anything. All this enthusiasm at the provincial power authorities level was squelched by politicians. I ask hon. members why? I can tell you that no one knows the answer.
I talked to Mr. Levesque, now the Premier of Quebec, but was minister of resources in the Lesage government and he was enthusiastic. He was the first president of the Canadian Council of Resource Ministers. He said this was the only way the federal system would work, if we all sat down as equals and discussed what was best, and then do whatever came under our jurisdiction. What an opportunity Canada missed.
1 have another fact. You have heard me talk about wind power and you have heard me talk about heat pumps in this House, but I have not yet talked about one of our greatest resources in energy, namely, geothermal energy.
Geothermal energy is found in the Cumberland Basin. It runs right across to Gaspe. Geothermal energy is under southwestern Ontario, under the prairies and in isolated spots in British Columbia. We have no information about it in the north. But let me quote what scientists said two years ago. They said that on the prairies alone the energy content of this hot water beneath the prairies is 360 times the energy content of all the natural gas we will ever discover in Canada, and we have discovered a lot of natural gas in Canada. We still have 400 trillion cubic feet to come that we know about. But geothermal energy is 360 times greater. Geothermal energy can be turned on site into electrical power and sent anywhere, north, south, east or west. Think what security we could bring to the manufacturing province of Ontario. We could send that power east, west, north or south because we know we could get it back under this concept of moving power around to meet time zones east and west and to meet the peak loads north and south. I will not go through all the technical data about that.
1 have not put a figure of energy content on the 250 billion tons of coal. I could do it, but I am simply saying that Canada has energy of a non-renewable sort running out of our ears. We sit in this House and fight and quarrel like a group of children over a silly little bit of oil, which is only going to last five years anyway. I would not like to see this Parliament continue dealing, as it is now with oil prices, because of this pride of confrontation which exists between politicians. One of the ways to settle this darned thing is to quit fooling around. Everyone knows that a power grid, which would have cost $300 million in 1963, with the knowledge we have today would only cost about $1 billion, would move power in tremendous volumes back and forth, way below the cost of what we have to pay for energy from local sources today.
We are no longer talking about $2-per-barrel oil in determining whether the project has a benefit cost ratio plus. We are talking about $30 and $50 for a barrel of oil. If we want to face this $30 and $50 per barrel of oil, we should just sit and wonder about these things.
Let us talk about all the things we have looked at. I have not seen the 1977 report.
If we had wanted to use this great energy of Canada 25 years ago to build up the Atlantic region to the highest level of any industrial complex in the world, it could have been done. It has all the markets of the world at its service, access to the Arctic resources by sea from the north, access to all of this energy in their own area and, with a labour force as good as any in the world, it should be one of the richest complexes in the world. Had we started that 20 years ago, what regrets would those of us have today who knew what the hopes were then? We have to face up to this and get it done.
I want to see an east-west power grid so that British Columbia, Manitoba and Quebec are not forced to sell south. That is the only way to finance their operations today with the high cost of energy. I would like to see these great unused power resources built in.
There is no use talking about Fundy tides if you are talking about a market in the Atlantic area. It needs a market 1,000 miles in diameter, and when those great surges come four times a day let the high voltage lines be built that will pump it out and bring it back so the whole area becomes secure. If we happen to help 100 million Americans in the process, so be it. We will get it cheaper; it is ours. This is what sharing means; this is what co-operation means.
I appeal to members on the government side to go after the department and ask for a copy of the 1963 report. No member of Parliament has seen it. Let us look at it. Let us apply the new cost figures to it. Take the report and study of 1977 and let those who know something about it look at it. Do not let these reports be taken as an excuse to avoid action. Do not bury them, bring them out into the daylight. It is amazing how many people across this country cry in their beer at night, thinking of all the work they did some 20 years ago. I have had them come into my office and show me the different parts of the report which they did. Why not let it be known, that is all we ask. Get the information out. Once you see there is a market for this great power of Fundy, the tidal power from other areas and all the other forms of energy across the country, there is no question about what the decision will be. If you want to fight inflation and energy costs, the key to it over the next 30 to 50 years will be this power grid. Let's look at it; let's get it moving.
The suggestion of calling a meeting is fine. Restore the old Canadian council of resource ministers or any group that will meet together. The various provincial ministers are not dolts. They would like to work together. However, they need the leadership of the federal government which seems reluctant to think big. That is the job of this House. If the members of this Parliament do nothing but get them back together again and start talking, if we make that contribution in the next three or four years, we will have served our country well.
February 16, 1981

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on the motion before us. I wish to clearly indicate that the members of the New Democratic Party have no hesitation in supporting the principles enunciated in the resolution. We believe the study and the eventual establishment of a national power grid would be just part of what we conceive as a major need in this country, the establishment of an industrial strategy to use the material and human resources to the benefit of all people, to meet their needs and provide the required jobs. In order to have an industrial strategy, we need planning on a major scale by the federal government in co-operation with the provincial governments.
One of the major resources in this country is hydroelectric power. Although we probably use more hydroelectric power per capita than any other country in the world, we have tremendous unused and untapped sources in northern Quebec, northern Manitoba, northern British Columbia and other places.
As the hon. member who introduced the resolution is from Atlantic Canada, he talked about the resources of Labrador and the Bay of Fundy. There are tremendous resources in western Canada. The Conservative Premier of Manitoba is talking about a power grid among the three prairie provinces.
These potential resources should be studied in detail, catalogued and used to the utmost. Hydroelectric power should be used as much as possible in place of our non-renewable resources such as oil, natural gas and coal. That cannot be done without a study and a national grid which would connect the sources of power we now have.
It makes no sense for Labrador power to be sold to Quebec and then to the United States rather than to New Brunswick, Nova Scotia or Ontario. It makes no sense for Manitoba to sell power to the United States when it could and should be selling to Saskatchewan or Alberta thereby obviating the need for the coal they now use. We support this bill in principle and hope it receives the support of the House.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL POWER GRID
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have this opportunity to speak on the motion of the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester (Mr. Coates). It fits in very well with the objectives of the National Energy Program to move away from expensive and insecure oil to electricity, natural gas, biomass and other renewable energy sources.
During the past 20 years we have seen a number of interconnections between northern and southern British Columbia, the Nelson River transmission system between northern Manitoba and the south, an interconnection into the United States between the eastern and western parts of Ontario, the eastern and western parts of Quebec, an interconnection between Quebec and New Brunswick and the cable system to Prince Edward Island, as well as the interconnection between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. There were a number of interconnections established through co-operation between the provincial utilities and the federal government. In some cases funding was provided for interconnections between the various systems.
Borrowing Authority
In respect of exporting to the United States, it is very important to use utilities such as Ontario Hydro because of the tremendous power needs in New York City and New York state. This power is required for air conditioning during the summer months when our needs in Ontario are not as great. The load can be maintained and the exports take place. Very substantial financial rewards return to the utility in Ontario and there is a cost advantage for Ontario consumers.
There is a need for an interconnection between Saskatchewan and Alberta. With the very rapidly expanding economy of Alberta, there will be a need for an interconnection for the possible use of power from Manitoba. I understand an interconnection is being constructed between British Columbia and Alberta which will provide for the sharing of electrical resources between those provinces. It will make use of the hydro resources of British Columbia which are very extensive. Much is already being exported to the United States. There is a need for many interconnections.
We talked about the Fundy tidal power, the need for an interconnection between Labrador and Newfoundland because of the great potential of the Lower Churchill Falls system, and the ultimate possibility of exporting that power from the Lower Churchill Falls to the maritime provinces of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island.

speechtext: When the debate was interrupted at five o'clock, the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) had the floor.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was saying at five o'clock that the Auditor General had pointed out

February 16, 1981
Borrowing Authority
to the government many of the improvements that were necessary in order to return to fiscal sanity. We are now being presented with Treasury Board's recommendations of a review of information necessary for parliamentarians so they can have a rational review of expenditures. Appointments of departmental comptrollers have been too slow to assure that Parliament has the necessary departmental expenditure information.
The point of all these recommendations, and there are critics of them, is that these expenditures do not cost the government money. They save the government money. The faster this kind of thing can be put into effect, the better for all the taxpayers.
I want to refer to a conference I attended in Toronto, The Financial Post conference last year. It was called "Hands On, Hands Off'. A few words from Milton Friedman would probably be in order for my friends opposite. There were 300 delegates there, including two former ministers of finance from the government opposite. Mr. Turner, one of the former finance ministers, made a comment, as he was introducing Mr. Friedman, about completely free markets. I think he said they exist nowhere and that Canada was built with a judicious mix of private and public capital and initiative.
Mr. Friedman was quick to take Mr. Turner to task on that remark, pointing out that there is no such thing as public capital. There is only private capital. Government and public expenditures come only from wealth produced by individual taxpayers. He also had an answer for governments generally, about inflation, reminding us that it was caused by governments, governments that were too fastidious to finance expanding social programs by raising taxes or borrowing at going interest rates, and so they had been creating money at a rate that outstrips the economy's growth. Of course, there is a solution: restrain monetary growth.
There are other solutions that have been tried. One has been tried, by the government opposite, namely, wage and price controls. History proved that both here and in the United States that was not the solution. It gave temporary relief to problems of inflation.
It is easy to blame people for inflation. The government blames the world, the weather, foreign markets, anybody else. They blame labour. Some people blame labour, which is certainly not responsible by simply making attempts to keep up with inflation. Business cannot be blamed for trying to raise their prices to cover higher cost. Even the banks have been blamed for inflation; but because of inflation caused by these bad fiscal policies, they have to pay higher and higher rates to people who are willing to save in order that the money can be loaned out to people who want to borrow. Of course, they have to pay higher rates for that money.
We need less government. That is the problem. That would go a long way to providing a solution. The government we have must stop smothering business with regulations and by control- . ling prices; for example, prices of oil. We have other examples of the government getting into matters like Petro-Canada and buying Petrofina. Just a month or so ago, the government purchased a whole string of service stations in the city of Vancouver. 1 do not think the taxpayers really wanted all that
money to come out of their pockets to buy a string of service stations from which they were already getting good service.
We also need an overhaul in the tax system. We need an overhaul which would encourage savings and investment in Canada. The present policy of taxing illusory gains created by inflation discourages saving by taxpayers and encourages spending. That, of course, fuels inflation. The present system is unfair and inadequate.
I will give just a couple of examples. In 1978, according to the taxation book to which I referred earlier, 2,300 taxpayers making over $50,000 a year paid no income tax at all, and that number includes 96 who earned over $200,000 and paid no income tax. Can a system which allows that be fair?
Let us look at the rules which affect tenants versus owners of homes. The owner of a home pays no tax on his gain when he sells his home, and a tenant who invests his capital and pays rent is taxed at very high rates because he chooses to be a tenant and invest his capital.
There are no roll-over provisions which would allow one to sell a personal asset and buy another comparable personal asset. In case hon. members think only business people are concerned about roll-overs, let me remind them that some people probably have cottages, certain collections or other items they value which they may wish to sell in exchange for another, but there is no roll-over provision, and they will have to pay the full capital gains tax and then find that they are not in a position to replace those particular assets.
I have given some examples of why we have this bill before us now, and there are others. Perhaps before I finish I could just mention the Mirabel airport, which has been in the news recently. The original cost of Mirabel was about $600 million, which included $150 million to expropriate farm lands nearby. Now the Grits have decided they no longer need all that land around that airport, and they want to sell it back to some of the 2,200 families whose lands were expropriated. But now how do they decide to whom they are going to sell? Many of the home owners are gone. Some of the properties are leased to unsuspecting tenants, and some buildings are in disrepair, in spite of the fact that the government had a $10 million annual program to keep order in the general area. If we add all that to the $1 million a week being lost on the operation of Mirabel airport, we have an idea of why we have a bill like this before us.
It is clear that Liberal policies are leading us down the road to financial ruin, and there is no sign of needed changes, no sign of restraint from the other side, no sign of fiscal responsibility, no sign of fair taxation, no sign of reduced government interference, no sign of concern for individual taxpayers and no sign of concern for corporate taxpayers who, after all, get all of their ability to pay taxes from individual taxpayers.
With the policies of this government it is clear we will be back here next year, and maybe I will be taking part in a debate on another, bigger borrowing bill.
February 16, 1981

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak about the supplementary borrowing authority bill. Like other members of my party, I regret the imposition of closure, which denies to other members the right to speak on this issue.
This evening I would like to look at the supplementary borrowing authority from the perspective of my concern for the Indian people of Canada. We all know that the question of borrowing raises fundamental issues about the way in which this government is managing, or mismanaging, the economy, and we all know that the social fabric of our nation depends upon a healthy economy.
If ever we want evidence that the government has mismanaged the economy, we can find it by considering the plight of the Indian people. In many respects the Indian people are something like the miners' canary. When miners had to enter shafts where there was a possibility of dangerous gas or bad air, they used to take canaries with them. The miners knew that if the canaries survived, they could survive. They knew that if the canaries succumbed to bad gas, they had better get out of there very quickly.
When we look at the situation of the Indian people, we see that in many ways it forecasts and highlights the situation all Canadians are facing. Indian people suffer the highest unemployment in Canada. For example, Norway House in Manitoba has a population of 2,500, and of that population of 2,500 there are over 700 people listed as unemployed employables. We will not find these people listed in the regular statistics on unemployment which come out from Statistics Canada every month. They are not part of the 945,000 people about whom this government does not seem to be concerned. They are an additional number. There are no records kept of them.
The ratio of employed people to dependants in the Indian community is one to ten. Whereas in the rest of society it is approximately one employed person to two dependants. This gives some idea of the serious situation, and to maintain this pace or even keep up with this deplorable situation of one person in ten employed, the government will have to create some 13,000 new jobs in the next ten years. But the government is not even doing that, it is falling behind and this deplorable rate is getting worse. Instead of creating an average of 1,300 jobs a year to maintain this ten to one ratio, the government is creating about 1,000 jobs. Next year the situation will be worse unless something drastic is done.
Because of their remote locations most Indian communities suffer even more than others from the high cost of living, and Indian people are the ones who suffer most from cutbacks in government spending. Government policies over the last 100 years have destroyed the economic basis for self-sufficiency. The people have had to depend upon government grants, public works projects and welfare. In some Indian communities the social assistance rate is over 95 per cent. Migration of Indian people to cities over the last 14-year period increased from 15 per cent to 30 per cent. People try to escape from one kind of poverty only to end up in another. They turn from
Borrowing Authority
unemployment in one area only to find themselves unemployed in another.
When the government cuts back, the Indian people feel it most. I believe it is time, as we look at this borrowing authority, that we looked at what is happening to the Indian people because, like the miners' canary, the welfare of the Indian people has a message for all of us, if we can only understand it.
I was talking today to someone from the Union of New Brunswick Indians who was concerned about the cutbacks in that area. On only two reserves were there minimal increases. On some reserves there were cutbacks in their administration funds which equalled 62 per cent. This means they have to cut back on basic essential services like street lighting. At the same time they are concerned about advertisements in newspapers for senior management consultants at salaries of between $31,000 and $36,000 a year. They will have the job of helping Indian bands manage their programs more effectively. The government is cutting back with one hand, and with the other it is offering to pay consultants $31,000 to $36,000 a year to help these Indian bands manage. They can be experts on how people can survive on nothing, but they themselves will be getting very nice salaries. The Indian people asked where the money for this new consultant program will come from, and they suspect very much that it will come from some of the cutbacks they experience.
The total budget for 60 Manitoba bands is up this coming year by only $10 million, from $122 million to $132 million. That represents an increase of only 8 per cent at a time when the cost of living is increasing by 12 per cent. We expect that the Indian people will be able to get along with 4 per cent less than last year. The director general for the region has asked for a barebones grant of $159 million, instead of which only $132 million was made available. The department is putting a penalty on those Alberta bands which have resources of natural gas by pressuring them to use the revenue from these resources. Instead of using the revenue for development, they want them to use it to supply services which normally the department has supplied.
I was speaking to someone from a smaller reserve in Manitoba who told me that a year and a half ago these people took over the management of their own school. At present, they are providing services from grade one to grade nine, and they hope to expand. Now they face cutbacks. They presented full cost estimates, with which the department agreed, for $737,000. Instead, the department says that $610,000 will be available for the next year. They are $127,000 short for the operation of that school. The department agreed with their needs, it agreed with their estimates, but it said it was sorry, it had no money.
What I am saying is that the government has not managed its finances properly. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that these cutbacks are as wasteful as any of the wasteful expenditures
7316

February 16, 1981
Borrowing Authority
which some other hon. members like to draw to your attention. When we cut back on basic items such as education, we are being wasteful of our human potential. This reserve is having to cut back on its social development programs, social assistance and minor home repairs. In every way we expect the Indian people to do with less. These are the conditions which result from cutbacks. We have created a dependence for these people, and then we cut back. I submit that if the government were borrowing money to invest in the future of Canada and if it were borrowing money to invest in the future of Indian people, we would agree. But this is not happening. In real terms, federal expenditures for Indian people have increased by 15 per cent over the past decade, while federal expenditures for non-Indian programs have grown by 128 per cent per capita in the same time; a 15 per cent increase for the Indian people, 128 per cent for other programs.
The Indian economic development fund has been described by department officials as a fund of last resort, and truly people need to be desperate to apply for it. In the current quarter, the interest rate for loans under $75,000 is a modest 19.75 per cent, but for loans and portions of loans over $75,000, the interest rate is 21.75 per cent. This is the fund which we expect Indian people to use to get development capital so they can develop their communities, so they will not be dependent on welfare, and so they will not always have to be coming to the government for a handout.
Last fall, when this was brought to the minister's attention, he agreed it was a deplorable situation. I understand he was hoping very much there could be some kind of a true development fund established which would make money available for the Indian people. But the minister was not successful in convincing Treasury Board there was such a need, so the present pitiful conditions are continuing. In 1979 and 1980, less than half of the money which has been allocated to development was actually used for that purpose. Much of the rest was used to cover over-target expenditures in education and social services because the government is always cutting back and giving less than the barebones estimates. When there are cost overruns, the government dips into the Economic Development Fund and uses that money to cover these cost overruns.
This is the way we continue to perpetuate a dependence rather than helping the Indian people to establish a true system of development. While less than 4 per cent of the total budget of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is available for development purposes, over 20 per cent is used for social assistance programs. It seems we want these people to continue on welfare, we want them to continue to be dependants rather than to give them the resources they need to develop their communities and develop economic self-sufficiency. I suggest that instead of the government using its borrowing power to allow the Indians to reach self-sufficiency and economic independence, it uses it to create a system of welfare dependence.
We have all seen the report of the Auditor General for the past year in which he indicates very clearly that the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is out of control and does not know what it is doing.The report states:
An example of the effect of these planning and control weaknesses can be found in the implementation of the policy for transferring program delivery responsibilities to Indian bands. We found that the department had not forecast the rate of transfer, nor were conditions for transfer specified.
When they found that costs had increased, they decided to implement cutbacks, and the Indian people are in the unhappy position of having to administer their own misery.
With regard to the Economic Development Fund, the report points out that:
-the department has approved loans totalling $81 million.
It does not know where they are going. It has had to write-off $17 million. The report goes on to state:
In our view, a significant portion of these proposed write-offs is due to the department's inadequate management of the approval of loans, monitoring of projects and collection of loans,-
There is a confusion of roles in the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. It does not know whether its job is to keep the Indians in line or whether its task is to help them with development. In October of 1980, officials of the department estimated that some $10 million was needed to help bands prepare for some of the massive development projects which would affect them in the near future. Last week they were offered $1 million. If the government is serious about the needs of the Indian people it will begin to shift its priorities from bureaucratic red-tape management and welfare dependence and begin to give priorities to economic and community development. This will cost money, and I urge that the government use its borrowing authority for this kind of a developmental purpose.
As a beginning it should adopt a clear policy for settling Indian band land claims in a manner which would give these people a base for their own economic development, and then it should institute a development fund which will give Indian bands access to capital. In this way they can use their resource base and their natural ability and have the capital to develop both.
We in our party very definitely oppose wasteful expenditures. We also oppose wasteful cutbacks, we oppose the waste of human resources and human potential about which this government does not seem to care, the waste that is represented by the more than one million people who are unemployed, and the waste that is represented by allowing our Indian people to exist in the backwater where no one pays any attention to them.
I want other speakers to have an opportunity to participate this evening, so in conclusion I urge the government to use its borrowing authority for positive purposes, not for a continuing patchwork of programs.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this particular debate. I guess all
February 16, 1981

hon. members in the House do not like the notion of shortening the debate but, on the other hand, when one is on this side- and 1 think the Tories would have experienced this had they been in power much longer-there is a very great need to move these things along. If we did not shorten debate at one time or another, I do not think we could possibly get done what must be done. I think this particular subject fits very well into committee. I will welcome it there, and I hope many members will participate at that level.
Part of what I have to say concerns what I would call neo-conservative mathematics. Those of us who have been involved in education, as I have been over 22 of the last 30 years, must feel that we are reaping the whirlwind of our own inadequacies when we must deal with this kind of mathematics. There always seems to be some kind of notion that one can just pull out an absolute figure, and that gives total meaning. For example, when we use an inflation rate of 12 per cent versus the inflation rate of 6 per cent or 7 per cent in West Germany-and I am not sure what it is at this particular point-we are dealing in figures which are relative, but we are not dealing with the base. I do not have any later figures but in 1978, dealing with an index on what can be bought, taking an index of 100 in the United States or 102 in Canada, and using the same currency in West Germany, one would get $150. It would be similar to a railway worker who may be new on the job. if he received a 10 per cent raise on his $10,000 income, his 10 per cent would amount to $1,000, but someone at the top end of the scale, such as an engineer, will go home with $3,000 as a result of the same 10 per cent raise. We have to be able to determine these bases.
The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) used a figure of $80 billion as the net national debt. She said that was very, very high. I have heard other members talking about the net national debt being $8 billion or $9 billion in 1960, comparing these two figures and saying, "Look at what terrible thing has happened." Of course, one must deal with the net national debt in terms of some figures to which one can have reference. For example, if I owe $10,000 it is very important, if I want another line of credit, whether my income is $5,000 or $100,000. It is very, very relative. There is no point talking about my debt of $10,000 without some base. I must have a base, and if I do not have a base of reference, then the figures are meaningless.
Similarly when we talk about the net national debt we must have a base. I always have a great deal of trouble when they talk about the gross national debt being $120 billion, the net national debt being $80 billion and the difference being $40 billion. Surely that is arrived at in a very, very devious way. The combined assets of the federal government must be worth more than $40 billion, certainly in terms of land, in terms of the north, and so on. However, that is not the argument at this particular point.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question will be very brief. For the benefit of the House, would the hon. member indicate what is the main thrust of his remarks? In effect, is he saying that we should be relatively happy with a 12 per cent inflation rate and a net debt position of $80 billion?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
The thrust of my remarks is not to say that we are happy. If the hon. member listens to my entire speech, I think he will get the thrust of my remarks. In fact, very shortly I will refer to an article which will provide the thrust of my remarks. Basically, it is that the doom and gloom which comes from the other side really does not make much sense. Nobody likes a gross national debt of $80 billion, but the point of the matter is that $80 billion represents 26 per cent or 27 per cent of the gross national product, and if we go back to 1962, it was about 30 per cent of the gross national product. It is the relative thing about which I am talking. That is what is left out of a lot of the neo-conservative comments, which I will illustrate in a minute.
I should like to look at the purchases of Petro-Canada. I hear people talk about some large oil company, such as Mobil or Gulf, buying and investing in the holdings of some other company; it may very well be the Thomson chain investing in Hudson's Bay. This is an investment. Thomson did not go out and spend $400 million or whatever; he invested it. When we went out and bought Atlantic Richfield in 1976, I believe we paid $340 million. I am told it is now worth about $1 billion. Is that a good investment? Certainly there must be a reason for it being worth a good deal more. Of course, I think one of the reasons is that all corporations in the oil industry are worth a great deal more. But in late 1978 or early 1979 I remember Morty Shulman saying to me on his show, "You threw away a lot of money; it was a waste of money", and today we are told that it is worth 2.5 times what it was then. If that is the case, how can one call it a bad investment? I would say that the people who sold it might very well have been skinned at that rate; if a company can appreciate 250 per cent in the course of two or three years.
It seems when the federal government purchases a company it is spending money. No one ever talks about the investment or what will be the return to Canadian people. They do not talk about those things. It is all right for the Alberta government to buy PWA; it seems fair enough. But when the federal government does it it is some kind of crime. Those mathematics always bother me.
Over the weekend when I was preparing for this particular speech, I noticed an article which appeared in The Globe and

February 16, 1981
Borrowing Authority
Mail. In fact I was surprised to find it in The Globe. I always suspect that Rupert Murdoch has secretly bought The Globe and it is now a new paper. At any rate, I should like to refer to the article by Lawrence Martin in Washington. He said:
Ronald Reagan tells the country it is in its worst economic mess since the Great Depression. He lofts a 1960 dollar on the television screen and, illustrating the nation's misery, demonstrates that it is only worth 36 cents today. He says that big government is at the root of most of the country's economic problems. He vows to take a meat axe to the budget.
Let us take a look at that in terms of American funds at this particular point in time.
In 1960 when a dollar was worth a dollar, the median family income in the United States was roughly $5,000 a year. In 1979, the median income was $19,000 a year. Nineteen thousand dollars worth 36 cents each comes out to $6,840 real 1960 dollars. In those terms, the standard of living, despite what the president tells the people, has risen sharply-by almost a third.
So, the American people are better off by a third. In 1960, in terms of 1971 fixed dollars, our gross national product was $53 billion. In 1975, in terms of 1971 fixed dollars, our gross national product was $110 billion. In that period of time we see a doubling. We can certainly say that Canadians are far better off than we were in 1960, in spite of the kind of thinking put forward by the Conservatives.
Mr. Martin in his article says:
Myth No. 2 that the new administration is trying to pass off is that big government and its deficits are the prime cause of inflation. The new-right Reaganites have such deep faith in this theory that it is the one prong of their one-pronged anti-inflation program.
Basically, that is what I have heard from the opposite side of the House since 1974-75. Mr. Martin in his article goes on to ask about oil prices and food prices.
At this point let us take Vancouver as an example. What about the land which is being bought by people from Hong Kong, and Alberta, which is pushing prices up tremendously? There you have a situation of tremendous tension brought on by super-inflation. It is not caused by government. These are real inflationary effects which are structural in nature. They can be defined very easily. The increase in oil by seven or eight times has a tremendous effect on inflation. To say that there is really only one inflationary factor does not make sense.
Mr. Martin's article goes on:
Myth No. 3 is that government has grown so big that it is out of control. In fact, government hasn't grown so much.

speechtext: What about total spending? Tell us about that.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
We are talking about the federal government's expenditures which tend to create spending.
Looking at another set of figures, let us see what has happened to government spending. President Reagan says that the great offender is the federal government. It has been shown that it is not the great offender. But let us take a look at what is happening in Canada, since members opposite seem to want to talk about that. Using 1960 as an example, federal government spending amounted to 17.0 per cent of the gross national product.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: What is it now?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
In 1979 it was 16 per cent. I am glad the hon. member opposite is asking these questions, since I have the answers right here. I talked before about having a reference point, which I think is very important. As I said, in 1960 it was 17 per cent of the gross national product and in 1979 it was 16 per cent.
Another interesting example can be found in the provinces. In 1960 provincial expenditures represented 6.1 per cent of the gross national product. In 1979 it rose to 15 per cent. What happened is that there was a growth in government spending by the provinces and the municipalities. Municipality spending has increased, but not by a great deal, as I see it. It has probably increased by about 5 per cent or 6 per cent over the particular period of time about which I am speaking.
What has really happened is that there has been a massive transfer from the federal government to the provinces and the municipalities. This bears particular importance when you consider the subject we will be debating tomorrow. The party opposite talks constantly about the power of the federal gov-
February 16, 1981

ernment and how we must maintain the power of the provinces. That is the basis of the difference between the constitutional views on this side of the House and what has been said opposite-certainly by the Tory party.
It is extremely important to realize that the growth of provincial government in terms of the gross national product has been at least infinitely faster than that of the federal government.
The only way power can be defined is by looking at who spends what. For instance, if we went back to 1943, which was a time of war and rather a poor period to look at, we would see that federal spending in terms of the gross national product was 22.3 per cent whereas the provinces spent 3.3 per cent.
Looking at 1955, the figure for federal spending was 17.6 per cent compared with 4.8 per cent for the provinces. I think this means there has been a relative shift in power from the federal government to the provinces. I think the new Constitution and the thinking on this side of the House reflects the need to reverse this.
The Economic Council of Canada spent a great deal of time looking at the relationship between the federal and provincial governments with respect to surpluses. In its seventieth annual review, page 60, it deals with the kinds of surpluses that exist between the federal and provincial governments. It shows that with the resource revenue being transferred to governments such as Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia, and with the surpluses that these provinces will have, basically the total of all government deficits will disappear in three or four years. By that time there will be a zero deficit at all levels of government in this country. Even today, deficits are being reduced in this way. What do we do with a $14 billion federal government deficit?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: Sixteen.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
ASH billion or $15 billion federal government deficit which, when put alongside the provincial surpluses, gives us a net surplus in terms of all the governments of Canada. That is the only way these things can be compared. It is the reference point that we must have.
As the future unfolds and as we deal with the Constitution and with a second phase, we will have to deal very seriously with the kind of distortion that has been created of a large federal deficit side by side with very large provincial surpluses. I think there will be a lot of debate on this situation over the next year or two.
1 want to conclude by saying that this is not just simplistic mathematics; it is not a matter of picking a number and saying, "that is it". We have to deal with these references, with these trends and the things that really count. A figure of 10 per cent or 12 per cent inflation has to be associated with the base and with the relative base of other countries and so on.
