speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak to the principle of Bill C-59, an act to provide supplementary borrowing authority, I am reminded that this is my first opportunity to speak since the change of government in the United States of America, our great neighbour. Therefore,
I should like to take a few moments to remember the six years I spent working in New York and Arizona, to congratulate President Reagan and his cabinet and to wish them well in the difficult years ahead. His conservative philosophy held for me a fascination and won my admiration during my U.S.A. political experience.
In recognition, also, I should like to pay tribute to retiring President Carter, irrespective of perhaps a somewhat different ideology. I do so, perhaps, because of our early common experience in nuclear engineering.
All members in this House recognize recently retired President Carter as a man who worked for peace among nations and know that during his term, America was not at war. During his term, the fundamental principles for world arms limitation were established and he laid a foundation for the evolution of a lasting peace settlement in the Middle East.
Furthermore, I am certain that all in this House, indeed all Canadians, recognize President Carter as a man of faith and belief in the fundamental human rights of all peoples and of the liberation of the human spirit of all economically and politically repressed peoples throughout the world.
More pointedly, let me deal with the borrowing Bill C-59 which is before this House. It is always unfortunate when we have to deal with legislation that has come under the sword of closure. This bill is an indictment of Canadian governments. The bill reminds us that our national government debt has exceeded $100 billion and that we are generating additional debt at between $14 and $15 billion per year. This is a national disgrace; indeed, it is a national tragedy. It is a shame, indeed almost treasonable, as the Government of Canada presides, in my estimation, over the richest nation in all the world. Only 23 million people share the ownership of this vast wealth of arable land, immense freshwater systems, vast untapped storehouses of minerals and hydrocarbon resources, forests, hydro potential, fish, wildlife and literally every kind of resource one can imagine. What a vast potential for wealth generation and yet we borrow and borrow. We are living off the backs and the sweat of coming generations. I would ask, why? It is because the government's management systems and the political guidance of this House over the last decade have failed economically. We have imposed a management system where wealth redistribution has throttled wealth production in a nation with unlimited economic potential. Repeatedly, Canadians today are worried about the future, about the changes to the Canada of the future brought about by the government's inadequate management policies, worried about inflation and the lack of an over-all effective industrial and social policy.
Let us look into the past a bit to see if we can gain some insight into where we are going. What have we done in Canada during the last 35 years since the war?

February 16, 1981
Borrowing Authority
In summary and in over-all perspective, I perceive the following to represent what we have done in building the Canadian society during the last three and a half decades.
First, we have educated ourselves, as a people, to one of the highest standards in the world. Our education has been broadly based with a wide and non-constricting and non-dogmatic perspective. It was moderately permissive and generally directive toward material rather than spiritual ascension. It predominantly, though not totally, followed the American mould.
Second, we applied technology extensively, most of it imported from the United States of America through the media of the multinational corporations, though we have excelled in a few areas like nuclear energy, on our own. Because we used extensively the multinational corporations and their access to American-developed technology, these corporations became dominant in owning our resources and industrial wealth. We became an intermediate manufacturing and exporting nation with declining competitiveness.
Third, economically, on an over-all basis, we have had phenomenal growth in our national economy, primarily based on harvesting and selling our vast resources. Our economy grew from a GNP of $31 billion by approximately four times in constant dollars during three and a half decades. Our population grew only by 75 per cent. We became rich as a nation though other nations surpassed our growth because of much greater productivity. We built in Canada a physical plant system of unprecedented inefficiency and only now are we realizing it as world energy costs are skyrocketing. We almost forgot that fundamental, applied and innovative research must be an integral part of a highly complex industrial society like ours.
Fourth, economically and socially, the nation experienced an intense preoccupation with security; security against almost every eventuality: sickness, unemployment, old age, catastrophe, business bankruptcy, and so on. Most of this security was backed or sponsored by government action. We built a humane society based on government redistribution of wealth. Our system adopted tenure as a right rather than a privilege tempered with responsibility. We provided undisputed tenure to our civil servants, professors, teachers, professions, and thereby generated an increasing demand for tenure without productivity requirements in all organized labour. With increasing tenure, productivity waned. We became lazy, and the pride of doing was replaced with the enjoyment of loafing. Elaborate procedure and refined specialization became a substitute for performance. We demanded more and more from our governments.
Fifth, we became preoccupied with enjoying all the material goods of life at an increasingly younger and younger age. Homes, suites, cars, goods of all sorts were demanded and promoted for the young. In providing all these goods, we established a vast credit system to give us what we wanted now, and increasingly mortgaged our future. Mass advertising created the appetite, credit provided the means, mass production and technology and imports provided the goods and lowered prices. We spoiled ourselves with obsolescence; redundancy, style, throwaway and fraud prevailed and is prevailing. Our appetite increased, our frugalness decreased, we damned the future and lived for the present. Governments evolved a taxation system of unprecedented complexity and unfairness. The poor are paying hidden taxes at every turn. The hidden tax load in Canada is excessive on such necessities as housing.
A few years ago when the Hon. Barney Danson was the minister of housing, I pressed very strongly at a conference of housing ministers for an analysis on the tax structure on housing in Canada. An intermediate analysis was done which found the tax load excessive. It was tax on tax on tax. The federal government did not conduct such a study. It shied away from it. Instead it laid out the terms of reference for the Greenspan study.
Sixth, we demanded more and more from our governments, and governments grew dramatically and involved themselves in every facet of our lives. Governments at the three levels grew without attention to political ideology, rationality or prudence. Politically, we have dashed madly toward de facto socialism with the three levels of government this year expected to tax 43 per cent of the gross national product of Canada. Governments have engaged themselves massively in wealth redistribution at rates which exceed the nation's ability for wealth production. Our appetite as governments is so voracious that massive debt formation has almost overwhelmed us.
The federal government deficit this year is expected to reach $15 billion alone. As debt rises, we print more paper money and so institutionalize inflation rates in double-digit figures. What is inflation? It is a reminder of the reality that we are living beyond our means, that we are getting poorer and must increase our productivity and competitiveness as a nation. We borrow more, we print more and delay the final reconciliation with fiscal prudence, but we shall not escape. The poor, the needy, the weak, the old, suffer the most during these terrible readjustment periods. The time for readjustment is upon us whether we know it or not. This borrowing bill is nothing more than an escape from fiscal prudence that is so vitally necessary.
Seventh, politically our nation has evolved peacefully. Partisan politics has become ideologically blurred with all parties moving significantly for greater socialization and greater government involvement in the economy, regardless of political direction.
One party in Canada had its vision of splitting the country fail. In my opinion, it will try again if given the chance. Out west we have an embryonic separatist movement but the durability of the nation shall prevail.
Provincial governments have grown and gained significantly in relative posture and prominence over the national government in some cases. The national presence and dominance has receded in economic terms but has ascended in emotional and communicative fervour. Some constitutional redefinition, reemphasis and redistribution are timely. Patriation of the Con-
February 16, 1981

stitution is a vital necessity. It has been delayed too long and permitted too many national and regional problems to accumulate.
Eighth, the world around us for a while grew in stability and then began to come apart at the joints. Political, social and economic instability is increasing. World-wide inflation is causing a severe form of economic dislocation. Economic issues resulting primarily from nationalistic protectiveness and resource-pricing policies are now foremost in the minds of world leaders. The risk that the operation of the international economy may spin out of control presents a graver threat to world order today than the nuclear arms race or the struggle between differing political ideologies. Democracy as a form of government is severely threatened by world-wide inflationary pressures.
As I see it, over the last 35 years, that in a nutshell was the situation both internally and externally and it is the situation facing Canada in the 1980s. One might ask, have we built our national economic house upon a rock or upon the sand? I think our living room is anchored on rock but our economic kitchen is on pretty slippery sand. We have many adjustments to make during the 1980s.
First, can we revise our economy and re-establish private enterprise as our motivating force for accelerated wealth production, or, at the least, can we find a workable and productive partnership between the private and the public sectors? I think we can. We are intelligent enough in Canada to do this irrespective of governments.
Second, can we contain the voracious appetites of governments and restrain their growth rates by re-establishing the community, the home and the family unit as the prime motivator, caretaker and babysitter of the social dislocations of our society? The Crosbie budget was the beginning of the movement in that direction.
Third, can we in the organized workplace rediscipline ourselves to increase productivity, innovativeness and deploy new technology to improve our competitiveness in the international marketplace? That was the intent and policy of the Progressive Conservative government a few months ago.
Fourth, can we control inflation and its ravaging effects upon the less fortunate? The Crosbie budget set a new direction in this regard, but some policies across the way may help in this regard in the future.
Fifth, can we meet the challenge of energy self-sufficiency in all forms of energy use? In particular, will we be able to meet the world food crisis resulting from environmental, climatic and population growth patterns?
Sixth, will we be able to cope with the inherent economic and social restratification needed to cope with an increasingly aging population? We must examine seriously our pension systems and anchor them to a more solid financial foundation than those to which they are now anchored.
Seventh, will we be reaching for greater brotherhood rather than increasing isolation in our urban conglomerates as we move toward a new century of civilization?
Borrowing Authority
Eighth, can we meet the challenge of constitutional patria-tion, redefinition and renewal in the 1980s? I think we can.
In conclusion, may I again say that this borrowing bill before the House is a reflection of the inadequacy of the Canadian government's management system. As governments, we do not manage the national economy well. We try to administer it through bureaucracy, a guaranteed process for moving toward bankruptcy. What we need is a national government with the vision, understanding and determination to right the national wrong in our country, a faltering economic system in the richest country in the world.

Mr. Speaker,
I thank my colleague from Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko) who just spoke. He covered many of the introductory remarks I would have made in addressing myself to this disgusting example of a government which has to stoop to borrow large amounts of money and to mortgage the future of our children. It borrows against the equity of the national resources of some regions of Canada in order to finance a style of government extravagance which is far beyond the ability of this country to pay in the short term. What we have from this government is another very poor example to the private sector and to the children whom we hope will grow up in this country knowing something about economic responsibility.
The statistics of borrowing and deficits of this government over the past decade have grown to horrendous proportions indeed. As a member from western Canada, I say that these statistics are depressing to all Canadians who know something about frugality, saving a penny for a rainy day. They do not believe in living beyond their means at the expense of their children in years to come.
The mood in this country is ugly. It is ugly because of the government's constitutional initiatives taken without regard for the sensitivities of the people in the regions, their premiers and Members of Parliament from those parts of the country not represented on the government benches.
The mood is ugly as well because people have had it up to their teeth with a government which fails to recognize the importance of restraint. It pretends, adopting the Keynesian philosophy of economics, that it does not matter if we incur these massive deficits because we will pay for them in the future with smaller dollars. In other words, it pretends it is incurring ever-increasing deficits on the notion that it is always easier to pay in the future than it is today. It is a sad commentary that the government assumes inflation as a given input for the justification of its deficits.
Much of what we are having to contend with is reflective of a tremendous misunderstanding of the concept of equality of opportunity on which this great country and our friend to the south, the United States of America, was based. The concept of equality of opportunity is quite distinct from the concept of equality of outcome. I wish to read some familiar words by a well known current author, one of the so-called neo-conserva-

February 16, 1981
Borrowing Authority
tives that my friend was referring to a moment ago. Milton Friedman writes, and I quote:
A society that puts equality-in the sense of equality of outcome-ahead of freedom will end up with neither equality nor freedom. The use of force to achieve equality will destroy freedom, and the force, introduced for good purposes, will end up in the hands of people who use it to promote their own interests.
That is what we are seeing in this country today, a system of patronage designed to benefit those who happen to be on the good side of the government in Ottawa, and disrespect and disregard for regions and political philosophies that may disagree with them.
How large is our deficit? The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) often uses an example. He points out that if any of us had the privilege of having a million dollars in the form of $10,000 bills, they would form a stack six or eight inches high. If you squash them down, your million dollars will be a stack of $1,000 bills only four inches high.
By comparison, if you stack those $1,000 bills to accumulate a total of $14 billion, which this government is asking to borrow, you would have a stack over a mile high some 7,000 or 8,000 feet high. If the net public debt in this country were changed into $ 1 bills and stacked up, they would reach to the top of the stratosphere, some 50,000 feet into the atmosphere, or 16,000 metres. That illustrates the dimension of the problem which faces Canadians and our children in the future.
I am alarmed that this government in its budget has shown no evidence of restraint, in total contrast to the sanctimonious-sounding promises in the throne speech of a few months ago. The government has shown no willingness to put into action the words expressed in the throne speech, and I quote:
My government will reduce the federal deficit in a planned and orderly manner .. . Improving the efficiency of the federal government is as important an objective of these reforms as reducing the deficit.
Balderdash! Where is the evidence shown to this House of improving the efficiency of the federal government? I will deal further with that in a few moments.
The government is spending 10 per cent more in the 1981 fiscal year than it spent last year, at a time when our gross national product is not likely to grow at all. If it does, it will grow by something less than 1 per cent. We keep hearing the myth in this House that things are bad all over, that times are tough in the United States and elsewhere. It is ludicrous for the Liberal members to blame the rest of the world, especially the Americans, for the serious plight of our economy.
All we have to do is compare the level of the U.S. deficit as a fraction of its government budget with our own to see the stark reality of the situation. The United States budget for 1980 was projected a year ago to amount to $600 billion, roughly ten times larger than our own. The projected U.S. deficit for that period was 3 per cent of that budget or about $16 billion, incidentally at the same level as our own.
It is now a year later and the Carter administration has left office. At the end of that year, Carter was projecting expenditures of some $663 billion, with revenue of $607 billion for a deficit of $56 billion. That deficit was only 8.3 per cent of
government spending in that very bad year as far as the U.S. administration is concerned. By contrast, this government is advocating a deficit in the order of 20 per cent of our government budget, a deficit of at least $14 billion in the present fiscal year. Our budgeted deficit of $14 billion out of $67 billion is three times as large as the U.S. deficit per capita and Ronald Reagan says he has a crisis on his hands.
There is indeed a crisis in the United States and they recognized it much earlier than we did. Our crisis is compounded all that much more, not merely because our deficit per capita is much larger, but because our economy is so intricately tied to that of the United States.
It is alarming to realize that this government and its finance minister have reverted to the old habits of the former minister of finance in his budget, the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien). In the budget presented in November, 1978, the government projected a deficit of $10 billion on a budget of $50 billion for a 20 per cent deficit.
When the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) came into this House and presented his budget in December, 1979, he put forward a budget for the 1980-81 fiscal year which reduced that deficit to only 14 per cent of his budget. By 1983 to 1984, the Conservative deficit would have been reduced to 6 per cent of budgetary spending. If we compare that with the projections of the present Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) we will find that for the same fiscal year, 1980-81, the Liberal budget shows we have gone back to a deficit in the order of one-fifth of our government budget, some $12 billion. For 1983-84, we have a deficit of some 9 per cent of projected government expenditures of $81 million. In other words, even by 1983-84, this government opposite is projecting a deficit one and a half times as large as that which the Crosbie budget projected. This is just totally unacceptable.
If one looks at that well-read report by the Economic Council of Canada called "A Climate of Uncertainty", and looks at Figure Chart 1-1 on page 8 of that report, he will find that of all of the governments in the western industrialized world, the Canadian government is the only one that reports an economy where the annual percentage of output is on the decline and has been continually since 1967. The other industrialized countries have, since 1973, shown a resurgence, a recovery in their economic output as measured by their gross national product. But this government and this country is contending with an ever-diminishing output as a percentage of gross national product and it just shows the extent to which our economy is in serious, serious financial shape.
In addition to the some $14 billion the government is asking to borrow tonight to add to the $80 billion gross net public debt, it is important government members realize what they are doing to public servants in this country, because they have now accumulated a $20 billion liability to all of the public service employees in Canada, and the armed forces, Department of National Defence, and the public service, generally. There is a $21 billion book liability to those government
February 16, 1981

employees and that liability is growing at the tune of $2 billion each year.
If you look at the budget introduced by the Minister of Finance in October, you will find, in table 1, on page 21 of that budget, there is an item "Annuity Insurance and Pension Accounts". This item amounts to some $2 billion, and this item amounts for the discrepancy between the Financial requirements of the government and its deficit. This government deficit is some $2 billion greater than its financial requirements because it has the benefit of a low-interest loan at the rate of four percentage points, compliments of the employees of the Government of Canada. I think that is shameful. I think the employees of the Government of Canada have been sold a bill of goods. They have been promised indexed pensions, but in fact their pension funds are growing at a rate three times the rate of outlay by way of payments to retirees. This government opposite, in a very scandalous move, is borrowing now to the tune of some additional $20 billion which adds to our present level of an $80 billion net public debt, and borrowing it out of the hides of the public servants of Canada. I think it is high time that question was addressed. Those employees are entitled to a properly accredited accounting as the Auditor General has demanded, and they are entitled to sit on a board of trustees to see those contributions secured in a form of equity so that they know, if faced with any possible range of economic circumstances, that the government has the ability to honour its commitments to those employees of the Government of Canada.

The hon. member may laugh, but he should remember that the Canadian population put their trust in this government and that, in the few months where his government was in power, it showed so much irresponsibility that it was thrown out by the Canadian voters.
During this period, increasing sources of funds from nonbudgetary accounts will help to finance the budget deficit of the government. During the second reading debate, the hon. members talked, of course, about the general direction of the economic policy of this government. However, they also referred to the national energy program. They talked about the authority to borrow in foreign currencies which is provided in this bill and which was also provided in the previous borrowing authority bill. They also talked about the direction of the monetary policy of the government, about the support given by the government to the Bank of Canada to reduce the money supply, about the impact of government deficit financing on private investment financing, and also about the debt structure in Canada.
During this debate, some members had the opportunity to explain why they disagree with this bill, and others to say why they support it. I would like to reply to some of the comments made during the debate, and I want first of all to refer to some of the points made by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). For instance, the hon. member said that the government has lost $1.1 billion by redeeming Canada Savings Bonds and attributed this redemption to a loss of confidence on the part of the citizens in their government. Mr. Speaker, the redemption of Canada Savings Bonds has a very different explanation from that given by the hon. member for St. John's West. In fact, the government is trying to reduce the part these bonds play in the total financing of the government borrowing operations or in the over-all management of the national debt. Moreover, if the hon. member for St. John's West would think back, he will remember that this was explained in detail in the Standing Committee on Finance,
Borrowing Authority
Trade and Economic Affairs when it studied the borrowing authority bill only a few months ago.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, Canada Savings Bonds can become a costly means of financing for the government. The interest rates on the bonds follow any upward adjustment of the interest rates payable in the marketplace. However, the downward movements of those rates are not reflected in the rate of return of the bonds. Furthermore, I would like to add that savings bonds are as good as cash since they can be redeemed any time at their face value.
Mr. Speaker, I see time is running short and I would like to deal with an aspect raised by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Wright) a few moments ago, namely, that hon. members do not have the opportunity to discuss what use the government will make of this money. I would like to remind him that hon. members not only have the opportunity to discuss what the government will do with this particular amount of money, that is the $14 billion in borrowings, but that they have many opportunities to discuss all government expenditures during consideration in committee of the estimates and also during the numerous sittings of the Committee of the Whole House on supply issues.
Mr. Speaker, I am satisfied that in the seven days of debate on this bill we have had ample opportunity to hear and consider the pros and cons with regard to this piece of legislation. We now know the position of the different parties on this borrowing authority. We will also have the opportunity in the standing committee, starting this week, to discuss further this borrowing authority and the management of the government debt.
